title: Atomic structure
objectives: Describe the structure of the atom: a tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around it
State the relative charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons, and how mass and charge are distributed in an atom
Predict how beams of protons, neutrons and electrons behave in an electric field
Work out the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in any atom or ion
Explain trends in atomic and ionic radius across a period and down a group
Define isotopes, use nuclide notation and explain why isotopes have the same chemical but different physical properties
Use the language of shells, sub-shells and orbitals, and write full, shorthand and electrons-in-boxes configurations (H to Kr)
Describe and sketch s and p orbitals, and explain what a free radical is
Define first ionisation energy, write equations for successive ionisation energies, and explain trends using nuclear charge, distance, shielding and spin-pair repulsion
Use successive ionisation energy data to deduce configurations and positions in the Periodic Table
prior: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons (IGCSE)
Electrons are arranged in shells, e.g. 2,8,1 for sodium
The Periodic Table is arranged in order of proton number, in groups and periods
Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons
why: Almost every idea in AS Chemistry, from bonding and shapes of molecules to periodic trends and redox, is explained by where electrons are and how strongly the nucleus holds them. This chapter gives you that toolkit. It also carries easy marks: Paper 1 usually opens with two or three questions from this chapter.
intro: Chemistry happens at the edge of the atom. Nuclei do not change in chemical reactions; electrons are shared, transferred and rearranged. In this chapter you will build a precise picture of the atom: what it is made of, how its electrons are arranged in shells, sub-shells and orbitals, and how much energy it takes to pull those electrons away.

sections.title: Particles in the atom and atomic radius

blocks.h: An atom is mostly empty space. Almost all of its mass is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons (together called nucleons). Electrons occupy shells (energy levels) in the space around the nucleus. If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea on the centre spot.

blocks.alt: Diagram of an atom: a small central nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electron shells
blocks.cap: Not to scale: the nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller than the atom.
blocks.h: <svg viewBox='0 0 420 260' width='100%' style='max-width:420px'><circle cx='210' cy='130' r='110' fill='none' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-dasharray='5 5'/><circle cx='210' cy='130' r='65' fill='none' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-dasharray='5 5'/><circle cx='202' cy='126' r='9' fill='#e11d48'/><circle cx='218' cy='126' r='9' fill='#64748b'/><circle cx='210' cy='139' r='9' fill='#e11d48'/><circle cx='210' cy='65' r='7' fill='#2563eb'/><circle cx='275' cy='130' r='7' fill='#2563eb'/><circle cx='100' cy='130' r='7' fill='#2563eb'/><circle cx='320' cy='130' r='7' fill='#2563eb'/><text x='240' y='160' font-size='14' fill='#0f172a'>nucleus</text><text x='325' y='112' font-size='14' fill='#2563eb'>electron</text><g font-size='13'><circle cx='20' cy='230' r='6' fill='#e11d48'/><text x='30' y='235'>proton</text><circle cx='100' cy='230' r='6' fill='#64748b'/><text x='110' y='235'>neutron</text><circle cx='185' cy='230' r='6' fill='#2563eb'/><text x='195' y='235'>electron</text></g></svg>

So the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus, and the nucleus carries all the positive charge. The negative charge is spread through the much larger volume occupied by the electrons. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It identifies the element.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
number of neutrons = A − Z
Counting particles in atoms and ions

Protons come from the proton number. Neutrons are nucleon number minus proton number. For electrons, start from the protons and adjust for the charge: a positive ion has lost electrons, a negative ion has gained them. One rule covers both: electrons = protons − charge (so a 2− ion has protons + 2 electrons).

blocks.q: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in the ion <sup>56</sup>Fe<sup>3+</sup> (Z = 26)?
steps: Electrons = 26 − 3 = 23 (a 3+ ion has lost three electrons)
blocks.err: Using the charge on the nucleus side: the charge never changes the number of protons.

blocks.q: A hydroxide ion contains <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>16</sup>O. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does OH<sup>−</sup> contain?
blocks.err: Forgetting that ordinary hydrogen (<sup>1</sup>H) has no neutrons.

blocks.q: How many electrons are in a <sup>32</sup>S<sup>2−</sup> ion? (Z = 16)
blocks.why: A 2− ion has gained two electrons: 16 + 2 = 18.

blocks.h: Add or remove protons, neutrons and electrons. Watch the element, charge, nuclide notation and shells change. Press Challenge me for a target to build.
Beams of particles in an electric field
When beams of protons, neutrons and electrons travel at the same velocity between two oppositely charged plates:

items: Neutrons have no charge, so they pass straight through, undeflected.
Protons (positive) bend towards the negative plate.
Electrons (negative) bend towards the positive plate, and are deflected much more than protons because their mass is about 1/1836 of a proton's.
In general, the angle of deflection is proportional to charge ÷ mass. For example, 4He2+ (2 ÷ 4 = 0.5) is deflected more than 7Li+ (1 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.14).

blocks.alt: Electric field diagram: electrons curve strongly towards the positive plate, neutrons go straight, protons curve gently towards the negative plate

Atomic and ionic radius

Across a period, atomic radius decreases. Each element has one more proton, so the nuclear charge increases, but the extra electron goes into the same shell, so shielding hardly changes. The outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.

Down a group, atomic radius increases. Each element has an extra shell of electrons, further from the nucleus, and more inner shells shield the outer electrons. This outweighs the increase in nuclear charge.

Positive ions are smaller than their atoms: in Period 3 metals the ion has lost its whole outer shell (Na 2,8,1 → Na+ 2,8), and the remaining electrons are pulled in more strongly. Negative ions are larger than their atoms: the added electrons increase repulsion between electrons, while the nuclear charge stays the same.

Across Period 3: cation radius decreases Na+ > Mg2+ > Al3+ (same electron arrangement, increasing nuclear charge). Anions are much larger than cations, and anion radius also decreases P3− > S2− > Cl− for the same reason. Down a group, ionic radius increases because each ion has an extra shell.

For isoelectronic species (same number of electrons, e.g. O2−, F−, Ne, Na+, Mg2+), use one argument only: same electrons and shielding, so the species with more protons is smaller. The order of radius is O2− > F− > Ne > Na+ > Mg2+.

blocks.wrong: Atoms get bigger across a period because they have more electrons.
blocks.right: Across a period the extra electrons enter the same shell, while the nuclear charge increases, so the atoms get smaller.

blocks.q: Drag into order of increasing radius (smallest first):
items: Mg<sup>2+</sup>
Na<sup>+</sup>
Ne
F<sup>−</sup>

blocks.h: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

Isotopes are written in nuclide notation: the nucleon (mass) number at the top left and the proton number at the bottom left, for example 3517Cl and 3717Cl. Chlorine-35 has 18 neutrons; chlorine-37 has 20.
Same chemical properties: chemical reactions involve electrons. Isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons, in the same electronic configuration, so they react in the same way.

Different physical properties, limited at AS to mass and density: isotopes have different numbers of neutrons, so their atoms have different masses. For example, heavy water, 2H2O, is denser than ordinary water.

blocks.wrong: Isotopes have different chemical properties because they have different masses.
blocks.right: Chemical properties depend on electronic configuration, which is the same for all isotopes of an element. Only mass-related physical properties, such as density, differ.

items: Isotopes of an element have the same nucleon number.
They have the same proton number but different nucleon numbers.
<sup>12</sup>C and <sup>14</sup>C have the same number of electrons in their atoms.
Both have 6 protons, so neutral atoms have 6 electrons.
<sup>37</sup>Cl<sub>2</sub> has a higher density than <sup>35</sup>Cl<sub>2</sub> under the same conditions.
Same number of molecules per volume, but each molecule is heavier.
Deuterium reacts with oxygen to form a different compound from hydrogen.
It forms water (D<sub>2</sub>O): the same reaction, the same type of compound.

sections.title: Electrons, energy levels and atomic orbitals

blocks.h: Electrons are arranged in shells (energy levels), numbered by the principal quantum number, n (n = 1, 2, 3, 4…). Each shell is divided into sub-shells (s, p, d), and each sub-shell is made of orbitals.
A region of space around the nucleus that can hold up to two electrons, with opposite spins.
Order of filling
In the ground state, electrons occupy the lowest-energy sub-shells available. The order of increasing energy is:
1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p
Notice that 4s is filled before 3d, because in atoms up to calcium the 4s sub-shell is lower in energy. Two more rules decide how electrons go into orbitals:

items: Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons, with opposite spins.

Within a sub-shell, electrons occupy orbitals singly first, with parallel spins, before pairing up. Electrons repel each other, so they keep apart in separate orbitals when they can (this minimises inter-electron repulsion).

blocks.h: Writing configurations

blocks.cap: Three ways to show the configuration of iron (Z = 26)
head: convention
iron
rows:
[Ar] ↑↓↑↑↑↑  ↑↓
3d                     4s

blocks.h: Two exceptions in the first row of the d-block: chromium is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 and copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1. A half-filled or completely filled 3d sub-shell gives a more stable arrangement.
Configurations of ions

For main-group ions, add or remove electrons from the highest-energy sub-shell: Na+ is 1s2 2s2 2p6; Cl− is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6. For transition element ions, the 4s electrons are removed first, before any 3d electrons.

blocks.q: Write the shorthand configuration of Cr<sup>3+</sup> (Z = 24).
blocks.err: Writing [Ar] 3d<sup>1</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>: taking electrons from the 3d first.

blocks.q: How many unpaired electrons does a sulfur atom have?
steps: 3p4 in boxes: ↑↓↑↑ (single occupation first, then pairing)
blocks.err: Pairing all four 3p electrons in two orbitals: electrons occupy orbitals singly first.

Shapes of s and p orbitals

blocks.alt: An s orbital is a sphere centred on the nucleus. The three p orbitals are dumbbell shapes along the x, y and z axes.
blocks.cap: s orbitals are spherical; each p sub-shell has three dumbbell-shaped orbitals at right angles (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>, p<sub>z</sub>).
blocks.h: <svg viewBox='0 0 480 200' width='100%' style='max-width:480px'><circle cx='80' cy='100' r='55' fill='#bae6fd' stroke='#0284c7' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='80' cy='100' r='3' fill='#0f172a'/><text x='70' y='190' font-size='15'>s</text><g transform='translate(300,100)'><line x1='-130' y1='0' x2='130' y2='0' stroke='#94a3b8'/><line x1='0' y1='-90' x2='0' y2='90' stroke='#94a3b8'/><ellipse cx='-45' cy='0' rx='42' ry='22' fill='#fecaca' stroke='#dc2626' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='45' cy='0' rx='42' ry='22' fill='#fecaca' stroke='#dc2626' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='0' cy='-45' rx='18' ry='38' fill='#bbf7d0' stroke='#16a34a' stroke-width='2' opacity='.85'/><ellipse cx='0' cy='45' rx='18' ry='38' fill='#bbf7d0' stroke='#16a34a' stroke-width='2' opacity='.85'/><text x='95' y='-8' font-size='14' fill='#dc2626'>pₓ</text><text x='8' y='-80' font-size='14' fill='#16a34a'>p<tspan baseline-shift='sub' font-size='10'>y</tspan></text></g><text x='285' y='190' font-size='15'>p (two of the three shown)</text></svg>
Higher-shell s orbitals are larger spheres: 2s is bigger than 1s. When drawing a p orbital in an exam, draw two equal lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus along one axis.
A species with one or more unpaired electrons, for example a chlorine atom, Cl•.

blocks.wrong: A p orbital can hold six electrons.
blocks.right: A p sub-shell holds six electrons, in three p orbitals. Every orbital, of any type, holds a maximum of two.
The 4s electrons are lost first: Fe<sup>2+</sup> is [Ar] 3d<sup>6</sup>.

blocks.q: Match each species to its configuration:
Which element has an atom with exactly three unpaired electrons in its ground state?
blocks.why: P is [Ne] 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup>: three 3p electrons in three separate orbitals.

blocks.h: The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms of an element, to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
Na(g) → Na<sup>+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup>    IE<sub>1</sub> = +496 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
Successive ionisation energies remove further electrons one at a time, always from gaseous ions:
Na<sup>+</sup>(g) → Na<sup>2+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup>   (IE<sub>2</sub>)     Na<sup>2+</sup>(g) → Na<sup>3+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup>   (IE<sub>3</sub>)
Ionisation energies are always endothermic (positive): energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron.
Four factors

head: factor
effect on IE
why
rows: shielding by inner shells and sub-shells
inner electrons repel the outer electron and reduce the effective nuclear attraction
an electron sharing an orbital is repelled by its partner, so is easier to remove

blocks.h: Trend across a period

The general trend is an increase across the period: nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell with similar shielding, so the outer electron is held more strongly. There are two small drops:

items: Mg → Al: aluminium's outer electron is in a 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than 3s and slightly shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove.
P → S: in sulfur (3p4) the electron removed is in a doubly occupied 3p orbital. Spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove than phosphorus's unpaired 3p electron.

blocks.h: Period 2 shows exactly the same pattern, with drops at Be → B and N → O.
Trend down a group

First ionisation energy decreases down a group (for example Li 520, Na 496, K 419 kJ mol−1). The outer electron is in a shell further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells. This outweighs the larger nuclear charge.
Successive ionisation energies

blocks.title: Successive ionisation energies of sodium (log scale)

blocks.h: Each successive ionisation energy is larger, because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion with less electron–electron repulsion. Big jumps appear when an electron is removed from a new shell closer to the nucleus. For sodium the jumps come after the 1st electron (2,8,1) and after the 9th (2,8,1): the pattern 1, 8, 2 matches its shells.

blocks.name: ie
blocks.title: Ionisation energy explorer
blocks.h: Real (NIST) ionisation energies for every element from H to Kr. Find the big jumps, solve a mystery element, and compare first ionisation energies across periods and down groups.

Count the electrons removed before the first big jump. That number is the number of outer-shell electrons, which gives the group (Groups 1 and 2: 1 and 2; Groups 13–18: 3 to 8). The number of jumps tells you how many shells, so the period.

blocks.q: The first five ionisation energies of element X (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) are 590, 1145, 4912, 6491, 8153. Which group is X in?
steps: The big jump is between the 2nd and 3rd
So X has 2 outer electrons: Group 2 (these are calcium's values)
blocks.err: Saying Group 3 because the jump appears at the 3rd value. Count the values before the jump.

blocks.q: Explain why the second ionisation energy of sodium is much larger than that of magnesium.
blocks.a: Na<sup>+</sup> is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>: its second electron comes from the 2p sub-shell, in the second shell, much closer to the nucleus and with less shielding. Mg<sup>+</sup> is [Ne] 3s<sup>1</sup>: its second electron comes from the third shell. So the electron removed from Na<sup>+</sup> is attracted much more strongly.

blocks.wrong: Noble gases have high ionisation energies because they are stable.
blocks.right: "Stable" is not an explanation. Use the factors: across a period nuclear charge increases with similar shielding and distance, so the attraction for the outer electron is greatest for the noble gas.

blocks.wrong: The drop from P to S is because sulfur has more electrons.
blocks.right: It is because sulfur's fourth 3p electron is paired; spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove.

blocks.q: Which equation represents the third ionisation energy of aluminium?
blocks.why: The third IE removes one electron from each gaseous 2+ ion.

summary: The nucleus is tiny and dense, contains protons and neutrons, and holds nearly all the mass and all the positive charge.
Neutrons = A − Z; electrons = protons − charge.
In an electric field: neutrons undeflected; protons to −; electrons to + and much more; deflection ∝ charge/mass.
Radius decreases across a period (more protons, same shell) and increases down a group (more shells). Cations are smaller and anions larger than their atoms.
Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons. Same chemistry (same electrons); different mass and density.
Orbitals hold 2 electrons with opposite spins. s: 1 orbital (2 e⁻); p: 3 (6 e⁻); d: 5 (10 e⁻).
Filling order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p; fill orbitals singly before pairing; Cr and Cu are 3d⁵4s¹ and 3d¹⁰4s¹; transition metal ions lose 4s electrons first.
s orbitals are spherical; p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y and z. A free radical has one or more unpaired electrons.
IE₁: energy to remove one electron from each atom in 1 mol of gaseous atoms to give 1 mol of gaseous 1+ ions.
IE depends on nuclear charge, distance, shielding and spin-pair repulsion. It rises across a period (drops at Group 13 and Group 16) and falls down a group.
Big jumps in successive IEs show a new, inner shell: count the values before the first jump to find the group.

flash.q: What is the relative mass and charge of an electron?
flash.a: Mass 1/1836 (negligible); charge −1

flash.q: Define proton number.
flash.a: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom

flash.q: Define nucleon (mass) number.
flash.a: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus

flash.q: How do you find the number of neutrons?
flash.a: Nucleon number − proton number (A − Z)

flash.q: Electrons in a 3− ion with 15 protons?
Which way do electrons bend between charged plates?
flash.a: Towards the positive plate, more than protons, because their mass is tiny

flash.q: What decides the size of deflection in an electric field?
flash.a: Charge ÷ mass

flash.q: Why does atomic radius decrease across a period?
flash.a: Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell with similar shielding

flash.q: Why is Na⁺ smaller than Na?
flash.a: It has lost its outer shell, and the remaining electrons are attracted more strongly

flash.q: Why is Cl⁻ larger than Cl?
flash.a: The extra electron increases electron–electron repulsion with the same nuclear charge

flash.q: Define isotopes.
flash.a: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons

flash.q: Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties?
flash.a: Same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration

flash.q: Which physical properties of isotopes differ (AS)?
flash.a: Mass and density

flash.q: Define an atomic orbital.
flash.a: A region around the nucleus that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins

flash.q: Number of orbitals in s, p and d sub-shells?
Order of sub-shell energy up to 4p?
flash.a: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p

flash.q: Configuration of Cr and Cu?
flash.a: Cr [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹

flash.q: Which electrons does Fe lose first when it forms ions?
flash.a: The 4s electrons

flash.q: Shape of an s orbital? Of a p orbital?
flash.a: s: spherical; p: dumbbell

flash.q: What is a free radical?
flash.a: A species with one or more unpaired electrons

flash.q: Define first ionisation energy.
flash.a: Energy to remove one electron from each atom in 1 mol of gaseous atoms to form 1 mol of gaseous 1+ ions

flash.q: Equation for the 2nd IE of calcium.
flash.a: Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻

flash.q: Four factors affecting IE?
flash.a: Nuclear charge, distance (radius), shielding, spin-pair repulsion

flash.q: Why is IE₁ of Al lower than Mg?
flash.a: Al loses a 3p electron: higher energy than 3s and partly shielded by 3s

flash.q: Why is IE₁ of S lower than P?
flash.a: The electron removed from S is paired in a 3p orbital: spin-pair repulsion

flash.q: Why does IE₁ fall down a group?
flash.a: Outer electron further away and more shielded, outweighing the extra nuclear charge

flash.q: What does a big jump in successive IEs show?
flash.a: The next electron comes from a new shell, closer to the nucleus

practice.q: Calculate the number of neutrons in one <sup>79</sup>Br atom and the number of electrons in a <sup>79</sup>Br<sup>−</sup> ion (Z = 35).
Write the shorthand electronic configuration of Cu<sup>+</sup> and of Cu<sup>2+</sup>.
practice.a: Cu<sup>+</sup> [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup>; Cu<sup>2+</sup> [Ar] 3d<sup>9</sup> (Cu is [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>; the 4s electron goes first)

practice.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of potassium is lower than that of sodium.
practice.a: K's outer electron is in the 4th shell, further from the nucleus, with more shielding from inner shells; this outweighs the greater nuclear charge, so the attraction is weaker.

practice.q: An element in Period 3 has successive ionisation energies (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>) of 1000, 2252, 3357, 4556, 7004, 8496, 27 107. Identify the element and explain.
practice.a: Sulfur: the big jump is between the 6th and 7th values, so there are 6 outer electrons (Group 16); Period 3 → S.

practice.q: State and explain which is larger: a sulfur atom or a sulfide ion, S<sup>2−</sup>.
practice.a: S<sup>2−</sup>: two extra electrons in the same shell increase repulsion between electrons, with the same nuclear charge (16+).

practice.q: Explain why <sup>35</sup>Cl and <sup>37</sup>Cl both react with sodium to form sodium chloride in the same way.
practice.a: Isotopes have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration (2,8,7); chemical reactions depend on electrons, not neutrons.

assessment.q: Which particle has the largest charge-to-mass ratio?
assessment.why: The electron has charge −1 and a mass of only 1/1836.

assessment.q: How many neutrons are in one molecule of <sup>2</sup>H<sub>2</sub><sup>16</sup>O?
Which species has the electronic configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>6</sup>?
assessment.why: Fe<sup>2+</sup>: 26 − 2 = 24 electrons, [Ar] 3d<sup>6</sup>. Fe is 3d<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>, Fe<sup>3+</sup> is 3d<sup>5</sup> and Co<sup>2+</sup> is 3d<sup>7</sup>.

assessment.q: Which element has the highest first ionisation energy?
assessment.why: N is in Period 2 (closer electrons than P and S) and has no paired 2p electron, unlike O.

assessment.q: Which atom has the most unpaired electrons in its ground state?
assessment.why: Cr [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>: 6 unpaired. Mn has 5, Fe 4, P 3.

assessment.q: Which statement explains why the atomic radius decreases from Na to Cl?
o: Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same.
Electrons are added to inner shells.
assessment.why: Electrons go into the same shell; the increasing nuclear charge pulls them closer.

assessment.q: The first five ionisation energies of X are 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577, 14 842 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. In which group is X?
assessment.why: Jump after the 3rd: 3 outer electrons, Group 13 (aluminium).
A chlorine atom has an unpaired electron.

assessment.q: Which property is different for <sup>6</sup>Li and <sup>7</sup>Li atoms?
assessment.why: They differ only in neutrons, so in mass (and density of the element).

assessment.q: Which equation represents the first ionisation energy of chlorine?
assessment.why: One mole of gaseous atoms forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

assessment_s.q:
Magnesium has three stable isotopes, 24Mg, 25Mg and 26Mg.
(a) State one similarity and one difference in the atomic structure of these isotopes. [2]
(b) Write the full electronic configuration of Mg2+. [1]
(c) Explain why the third ionisation energy of magnesium is much larger than its second. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) Same: 12 protons (and 12 electrons). Different: 12, 13 and 14 neutrons.
(b) 1s2 2s2 2p6.
(c) The 3rd electron is removed from the second shell (2p), which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded than the 3s electrons, so it is attracted much more strongly.

assessment_s.q: Sketch and explain the trend in first ionisation energy from sodium to argon, referring to the values for Mg/Al and P/S. [5]
assessment_s.a: General increase: nuclear charge increases, electrons added to the same shell, similar shielding [2]. Al lower than Mg: 3p electron is higher in energy / shielded by 3s [1–2]. S lower than P: paired 3p electron, spin-pair repulsion [1–2].

pp.mis: Mixing up neutrons and electrons in ions
pp.stem: Which species contains the same number of neutrons as an atom of <sup>16</sup><sub>8</sub>O and the same number of electrons as an atom of <sup>20</sup><sub>10</sub>Ne?
pp.exp: <sup>16</sup>O has 16 − 8 = 8 neutrons; Ne has 10 electrons. <sup>15</sup>N<sup>3−</sup> has 15 − 7 = 8 neutrons and 7 + 3 = 10 electrons.

pp.mis: Ignoring nuclear charge
pp.stem: Which process has the largest enthalpy change per mole?
pp.exp: Every ion on the left has the neon configuration 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>, so each process removes a 2p electron with the same shielding. The ion with the most protons, Cl (17+), holds that electron most strongly.

pp.skill: Successive IE data → group and period
pp.mis: Not using the size of the values to find the period
pp.stem:
X and Y are in the same group. Their 4th to 8th ionisation energies (kJ mol−1) are shown.
X: 7469, 10 990, 13 327, 71 330, 84 078
Y: 4556, 7004, 8496, 27 107, 31 671
Which row identifies X and Y?
pp.exp: Both show the big jump between the 6th and 7th values, so both have 6 outer electrons (Group 16). X has much larger values, so its electrons are closer to the nucleus: X is in Period 2 (oxygen) and Y in Period 3 (sulfur).

pp.mis: Confusing orbital with sub-shell
pp.stem: Which statement about s orbitals is correct?
opts: Every shell, starting from n = 1, contains one s orbital.
An s orbital can hold up to six electrons.
A 2s orbital is lower in energy than a 1s orbital.
pp.exp: Each shell has exactly one s orbital. Any orbital holds at most two electrons; 2s is higher in energy than 1s; s orbitals are spherical.

pp.mis: Placing the jump at the wrong electron
pp.stem: The first four ionisation energies of silicon are 787, 1577, 3232 and 4356 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. Which sequence could be the 5th to 8th ionisation energies of silicon (kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>)?
pp.exp: Si is [Ne] 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>2</sup>: four outer electrons. The 5th electron comes from the second shell, so there is a big jump at the 5th value, then a steady rise through the eight electrons of shell 2.

wrong.C: a second jump after only two electrons
wrong.D: the jump comes one electron too late

pp.skill: Combining IE data and group trends
pp.mis: Forgetting IE decreases down a group
pp.stem:
X and Y form an ionic compound Z.
X shows a very large increase between its 2nd and 3rd ionisation energies and has the second largest first ionisation energy in its group.
Y shows a very large increase between its 7th and 8th ionisation energies and has the largest first ionisation energy in its group.
What is Z?
pp.exp: X is in Group 2; IE falls down a group, so the second largest is the second element, Mg. Y is in Group 17 with the largest IE, the first element, F. Z is MgF<sub>2</sub>.

pp.mis: Adding the charge the wrong way
pp.stem: Which statement about <sup>81</sup><sub>35</sub>Br is correct?
opts: A Br<sup>−</sup> ion contains 46 neutrons and 36 electrons.
A Br<sup>−</sup> ion contains 46 neutrons and 34 electrons.
A Br<sup>−</sup> ion contains 35 neutrons and 36 electrons.
A Br<sup>−</sup> ion contains 81 neutrons and 36 electrons.
pp.exp: Neutrons = 81 − 35 = 46. A 1− ion has one extra electron: 35 + 1 = 36.

pp.mis: Miscounting the electrons before the jump
pp.stem: P and Q are in Period 3. P shows its first very large increase between the 1st and 2nd ionisation energies. Q shows its first very large increase between the 6th and 7th. What is the formula of the ionic compound formed from P and Q?
pp.exp: P has 1 outer electron: sodium. Q has 6 outer electrons and is in Period 3: sulfur. Na<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup> give Na<sub>2</sub>S.

pp.mis: Forgetting which sub-shell the outer electron is in
pp.stem: This question is about the first ionisation energies of sodium and argon. Which row is correct?
pp.exp: Argon has a much greater nuclear charge with the outer electron in the same shell, so Ar > Na. Sodium loses a 3s electron; argon loses a 3p electron.

pp.mis: Orbital vs sub-shell capacity
pp.stem: Which statement about a 2p orbital is correct?
opts: It can hold a maximum of six electrons.
In an isolated nitrogen atom, it contains one electron.
It is lower in energy than the 2s orbital.
pp.exp: N is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>3</sup>: the three 2p electrons occupy the three 2p orbitals singly. p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, hold two electrons each, and 2p is higher in energy than 2s.

pp.mis: Thinking nuclear charge explains it
pp.stem: Why is the second ionisation energy of lithium much larger than the second ionisation energy of beryllium?
opts: In Li<sup>+</sup> the electron removed is in the first shell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded.
Li<sup>+</sup> has a greater nuclear charge than Be<sup>+</sup>.
The electron removed from Be<sup>+</sup> is less shielded than the one removed from Li<sup>+</sup>.
Both electrons are removed from the same sub-shell.
pp.exp: Li<sup>+</sup> is 1s<sup>2</sup>, so its second electron comes from the first shell. Be<sup>+</sup> is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>1</sup>, so its second electron comes from 2s, further out and shielded by 1s<sup>2</sup>. Be actually has the larger nuclear charge, so B is false.

pp.mis: Thinking protons are removed
pp.stem: For the first 13 ionisation energies of an element, very large increases occur after the 3rd and after the 11th electron are removed. Which statement is correct?
opts: A proton is lost for each successive ionisation.
The element has only one outer electron.
pp.exp: Jumps after 3 and after 11 mean shells of 3, 8 and 2 electrons: 2,8,3. That is 13 electrons in total: aluminium. Ionisation removes electrons, never protons.

pp.mis: Pairing too early
pp.stem: What are the numbers of unpaired electrons in isolated atoms of B, C, N, O, F and Ne, in that order?
pp.exp: 2p<sup>1</sup> to 2p<sup>3</sup> fill the three orbitals singly (1, 2, 3 unpaired). From 2p<sup>4</sup> electrons pair up (2, 1), and 2p<sup>6</sup> has none.

pp.mis: More electrons = bigger, regardless of protons
pp.stem: N<sup>3−</sup>, O<sup>2−</sup>, F<sup>−</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> all have 10 electrons. Which has the largest radius?
pp.exp: Same electrons and shielding; N<sup>3−</sup> has the fewest protons (7), so its electrons are held least tightly and it is largest.

pp.mis: Using electronegativity or "stability"
pp.stem: Why is the first ionisation energy of oxygen lower than that of nitrogen?
opts: Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen.
In oxygen, the electron lost is paired with another electron in the same orbital.
The oxygen atom is larger than the nitrogen atom.
pp.exp: O is 2p<sup>4</sup>: the electron removed shares an orbital, and spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove. Electronegativity and anion formation are not ionisation factors, and O is slightly smaller than N.

pp.mis: Charge applied to neutrons
pp.stem: Which row correctly describes the ion <sup>39</sup><sub>19</sub>K<sup>+</sup>?
pp.exp: Neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20. Electrons = 19 − 1 = 18.

pp.mis: Assuming more protons always means higher IE
pp.stem:
Element X has a higher first ionisation energy than element Y.
Student 1: "X has more protons in its nucleus than Y."
Student 2: "X has a smaller atomic radius than Y."
Only one student is correct. Which elements could X and Y be?
pp.exp: F has a higher IE than Cl. F has fewer protons (student 1 wrong) but a much smaller radius (student 2 right). For N/C both statements are true; for Mg/Al and N/O neither is.

pp.mis: Changing the nucleon number
pp.stem: A nucleus of <sup>40</sup><sub>19</sub>K captures an electron, which changes one proton into a neutron. An atom of a different element, X, is formed. Which statement about an atom of X is correct?
opts: It has two electrons in its 4s orbital.
pp.exp: One proton becomes a neutron: 18 protons and 21 + 1 = 22 neutrons, nucleon number still 40. X is argon-40, [Ne] 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup>, with no 4s electrons. (Nuclear changes are not on the AS syllabus; the skill tested is particle counting.)

pp.mis: Counting electrons for the atom, not the ion
pp.stem: Which ion has the same electronic configuration as a neon atom?
pp.exp: Ne has 10 electrons. Mg<sup>2+</sup> has 12 − 2 = 10. Cl<sup>−</sup>, K<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup> all have 18, like argon.

pp.skill: Locating a shell change in successive IEs
pp.mis: Assuming the highest proton number always has the highest IE
pp.stem: Which of Li, Be, B and O has the largest third ionisation energy, and which has the smallest?
pp.exp: Li and Be both lose a 1s electron at their 3rd ionisation (very large); Be is larger because it has more protons. B<sup>2+</sup> (1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>1</sup>) loses its 2s electron and O loses a 2p electron from O<sup>2+</sup>; O<sup>2+</sup> has more protons, so B is smallest.

pp.mis: Misreading orbital occupancy
pp.stem:
Element Y is in Period 2; in its atom, the p sub-shell has two orbitals occupied, each by one electron.
Element Z is in Period 3; in its atom, all three p orbitals are occupied and two of them are full.
What is the formula of the compound formed by Y and Z?
pp.exp: Y: 2p<sup>2</sup> → carbon. Z: 3p<sup>5</sup> (↑↓ ↑↓ ↑) → chlorine. Carbon and chlorine form CCl<sub>4</sub>.

pp.mis: Ignoring the charge
pp.stem: Which species contains a different number of electrons from the other three?

pp.mis: Using the atom's electron count
pp.stem: What is the electronic configuration of the <sup>32</sup>S<sup>2−</sup> ion?
pp.exp: S has 16 electrons; S<sup>2−</sup> has 18, filling 3p. The nucleon number (32) does not affect electrons.

pp.mis: Not locating each jump
pp.stem:
The 2nd to 5th ionisation energies (kJ mol−1) of three Period 3 elements are shown.
X: 4562, 6910, 9543, 13 354
Y: 1451, 7733, 10 543, 13 630
Z: 1817, 2745, 11 577, 14 842
What are X, Y and Z?
pp.exp: X: already huge at the 2nd → 1 outer electron (Na). Y: jump at the 3rd → 2 outer electrons (Mg). Z: jump at the 4th → 3 outer electrons (Al).

pp.skill: Electrons in boxes for a transition metal ion
pp.mis: Removing 3d before 4s
pp.stem: Which shows the electrons-in-boxes configuration of Cr<sup>3+</sup> (3d then 4s)?
opts: [Ar] ↑↑↑
[Ar] ↑↓↑
[Ar] ↑  ↑↓
[Ar] ↑↑  ↑
pp.exp: Cr is [Ar] 3d<sup>5</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup>. Remove the 4s electron, then two 3d electrons: [Ar] 3d<sup>3</sup>, with three unpaired electrons in separate 3d orbitals and an empty 4s.

pp.mis: Charge changes neutrons
pp.stem:
Three statements about the ion 73Li+:
1 It contains three protons.
2 It contains four neutrons.
3 It contains three electrons.
Which statements are correct?
pp.exp: 3 protons; 7 − 3 = 4 neutrons; 3 − 1 = 2 electrons, so statement 3 is wrong.

pp.mis: Miscounting before the jump
pp.stem: The first five ionisation energies of element X, in Period 3, are 496, 4562, 6910, 9543 and 13 354 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>. What is X?
pp.exp: The huge jump is between the 1st and 2nd values: one outer electron, Group 1. In Period 3 that is sodium.

pp.skill: Counting neutrons from the mass number
pp.mis: Confusing mass number (a whole number of nucleons) with relative atomic mass (a weighted average, e.g. Co = 58.9).
pp.stem:
How many neutrons are contained in one atom of cobalt-59?
(proton number of cobalt = 27)
pp.exp: First, recall what the mass number means. The mass number, also called the nucleon number, is the total number of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus. Electrons are not counted, because their mass is tiny. The name cobalt fifty-nine tells us the mass number is fifty-nine. The proton number, twenty-seven, is the number of protons. Every cobalt atom has twenty-seven protons; that's what makes it cobalt. So the number of neutrons is the mass number minus the proton number. Fifty-nine minus twenty-seven gives thirty-two neutrons.

pp.skill: Finding the nucleon number of an ion
pp.mis: Adding the charge the wrong way round, and getting 21 protons for a 3− ion.
pp.stem:
An ion with a charge of 3− contains 18 electrons and 16 neutrons.
What is its nucleon number?
pp.exp: A negative ion forms when an atom gains electrons. So it has more electrons than protons. A charge of three minus means three more electrons than protons. So the number of protons is eighteen minus three, which is fifteen. Fifteen protons means the element is phosphorus, so this ion is the phosphide ion, P three minus. The nucleon number counts protons and neutrons, because both are in the nucleus. Fifteen plus sixteen gives thirty-one.

wrong.D: 21 protons: charge added the wrong way

pp.skill: Protons, neutrons and electrons in a polyatomic ion
pp.mis: Assuming isotopes change the number of protons or electrons. Only the neutrons change.
pp.stem:
A hydroxide ion, OH−, has a relative formula mass of 19.
How many protons, neutrons and electrons does it contain?
pp.exp: Start with protons, because they never change for an element. Oxygen has eight protons and hydrogen has one, so the ion has nine protons. Next, electrons. The charge is one minus, so the ion has one more electron than protons: nine plus one makes ten electrons. Finally, neutrons. A relative formula mass of nineteen means protons plus neutrons add up to nineteen, since electrons have almost no mass. Nineteen minus nine gives ten neutrons. As a check, an ordinary hydroxide ion made from oxygen sixteen and hydrogen one has a mass of seventeen. Nineteen means two extra neutrons, for example from the oxygen eighteen isotope. That doesn't change the protons or electrons.

pp.mis: Saying K<sup>+</sup> is smaller "because it has lost a shell". Compare it with Ar and Cl<sup>−</sup>: they all have the same shells.
pp.stem:
This question refers to isolated gaseous species.
Cl−, Ar and K+ are isoelectronic. In which order do their radii increase?
pp.exp: First, confirm they really are isoelectronic. Chlorine has seventeen electrons and gains one; argon has eighteen; potassium has nineteen and loses one. All three have eighteen electrons, in exactly the same shells. Because the electron arrangement is identical, the shielding is the same. The only difference is the nuclear charge: seventeen plus for chlorine, eighteen plus for argon, nineteen plus for potassium. More protons pull the same eighteen electrons more strongly towards the nucleus, so the particle is smaller. The potassium ion, with nineteen protons, is the smallest. The chloride ion, with only seventeen, is the largest. So the order of increasing radius is potassium ion, then argon, then chloride ion.

pp.skill: Charged particles in an electric field
pp.mis: Comparing only the masses ("lighter bends more") and forgetting that He<sup>2+</sup> carries double the charge.
pp.stem:
A 7Li+ ion and a 4He2+ ion are passed separately through the same uniform electric field at the same velocity.
Which paths do they follow?
pp.exp: First, the direction. Both ions are positive, so both are attracted towards the negative plate. That rules out P, Q and R. Each ion follows either S or T. Next, how much each one bends. At the same velocity, the deflection depends on the charge divided by the mass. A bigger charge means a bigger force; a bigger mass means it's harder to push sideways. For the lithium ion, the charge is one and the mass is seven, giving about zero point one four. For the helium ion, the charge is two and the mass is four, giving zero point five. The helium ion has the larger charge to mass ratio, so it bends more and follows T. The lithium ion bends less and follows S.

pp.mis: Counting only the outer s electrons, or forgetting that a full s orbital holds 2 electrons, not 1.
pp.stem: Which isolated gaseous atom has a total of exactly six electrons in spherically shaped orbitals?
pp.exp: First, the shapes. s orbitals are spherical, and p orbitals are dumbbell shaped. So we need the atom with exactly six electrons in s orbitals. Neon is one s two, two s two, two p six. The s electrons are two plus two, which is four. Sodium adds three s one, giving five s electrons. Magnesium has three s two, giving six. That's our answer. To check the last option, potassium is one s two, two s two, two p six, three s two, three p six, four s one. That's seven s electrons.

pp.skill: Electronic configuration of a transition metal ion
pp.mis: Writing [Ar] 3d<sup>3</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> for Fe<sup>3+</sup>, i.e. taking electrons from the last sub-shell written down.
pp.stem: What is the electronic configuration of the Fe<sup>3+</sup> ion?
pp.exp: Start with the iron atom. Iron has twenty-six electrons. After the argon core of eighteen, the 4s fills before the 3d, giving argon, three d six, four s two. Here's the key rule. When transition metal atoms form positive ions, the four s electrons are removed first, before any three d electrons. Once the 3d is occupied, the 4s electrons are the outermost and highest in energy. So to make iron three plus, we remove three electrons: both four s electrons first, then one three d electron. That leaves argon, three d five.

pp.mis: Forgetting state symbols, or starting from the element as O<sub>2</sub>(g) instead of single gaseous atoms or ions.
pp.stem: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of oxygen?
pp.exp: Start with the definition. The second ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous one plus ions, to form one mole of gaseous two plus ions. So the equation must start from the one plus ion, O plus, not the atom. That rules out A, which shows both the first and second ionisations together. Every species must be gaseous, so we need state symbols g. That rules out C, which uses aqueous. And the electron must be removed, so it appears on the product side. D shows an electron being added, which is the reverse process.

pp.skill: Explaining a difference in first ionisation energy
pp.mis: Writing "noble gases are stable" as an explanation. It earns no marks.
pp.stem: Which factor causes neon to have a higher first ionisation energy than fluorine?
opts: In neon, all the 2p electrons are paired.
Neon has a full outer shell, which is stable.
Neon has a greater nuclear charge, and the electron removed is in the same sub-shell with similar shielding.
Fluorine has more shielding than neon.
pp.exp: Write both configurations. Fluorine is one s two, two s two, two p five. Neon is one s two, two s two, two p six. In both atoms, the electron removed comes from the two p sub-shell. Same sub-shell means the same distance from the nucleus and the same shielding from the inner electrons. So D is wrong: shielding is not different. What does differ is the nuclear charge: nine plus for fluorine and ten plus for neon. Neon's nucleus attracts the two p electrons more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove one. Now the traps. Option A: paired electrons repel each other, which makes one easier to remove, so pairing can't explain a higher value. Option B: saying a full shell is stable describes the result, but it doesn't explain it in terms of forces.

pp.mis: Counting the jump position wrongly. The big jump is between the 3rd and 4th values, so there are 3 outer electrons, not 4.
pp.stem:
The first six ionisation energies of an element in Period 3 are shown.
1st2nd3rd4th5th6th
5781817274511 57714 84218 379
values in kJ mol−1
What is the outer electronic configuration of the element?
pp.exp: First, notice every value is bigger than the one before. Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion, so it's held more tightly. Now look for the big jump. From the third to the fourth ionisation energy, the value rises from two thousand seven hundred and forty five to eleven thousand five hundred and seventy seven. That's more than four times bigger. The other steps are much smaller. The big jump comes after the third electron. That means three electrons were in the outer shell, and the fourth has to come from an inner shell, much closer to the nucleus and less shielded. A Period 3 element with three outer electrons is in Group 13. That's aluminium, with outer configuration three s two, three p one.

pp.stem: Nickel is a transition element. The shorthand electronic configuration of nickel is [Ar] 3d<sup>8</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>.

parts.q: Give the full electronic configuration represented by [Ar].
ms: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup>

parts.q: Describe the shape of a 1s orbital.
ms: spherical (centred on the nucleus)

parts.q: Deduce the number of unpaired electrons in a nickel atom.
Complete the table for two isotopes of nickel: number of protons, number of neutrons and total number of occupied electron shells for <sup>58</sup><sub>28</sub>Ni and <sup>60</sup><sub>28</sub>Ni.
ms: <sup>58</sup>Ni: 28 protons, 30 neutrons, 4 shells
<sup>60</sup>Ni: 28 protons, 32 neutrons, 4 shells
1 mark for neutrons both correct; 1 mark for protons and shells both correct

pp.stem: This question is about the successive ionisation energies of phosphorus, P (Z = 15).

parts.q: Describe how the 1st to 7th ionisation energies of phosphorus change as each electron is removed. Explain the main feature.
ms: steady/gradual increase from the 1st to the 5th
a large jump between the 5th and 6th, because the 6th electron is removed from the second shell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded

parts.q: Construct an equation to represent the second ionisation energy of phosphorus.
ms: P<sup>+</sup>(g) → P<sup>2+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup> (state symbols required)

pp.stem: Beams of protons, neutrons and electrons leave a source at the same velocity and pass between two oppositely charged plates. Beam X curves sharply towards the positive plate. Beam Y curves gently towards the negative plate.

parts.q: Identify the particles in beam X and in beam Y.
ms: X: electrons; Y: protons (both needed)

parts.q: Suggest why beam Y is deflected less than beam X.
ms: protons have a much larger mass than electrons (about 1836 times), with charge of the same size

parts.q: Describe the path of the neutrons.
ms: straight through / undeflected, because neutrons have no charge

pp.stem: Boron is in Group 13. Its first four ionisation energies are 801, 2427, 3660 and 25 026 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.q: Use these values to state and explain (i) the general trend and (ii) the significance of the large difference between the 3rd and 4th ionisation energies.
ms: each IE is larger because each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion (more attraction / less repulsion)
the 4th electron is removed from the first shell (inner shell): closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so boron has 3 outer electrons

parts.q: Describe the distribution of mass within an atom of <sup>11</sup>B.
ms: almost all the mass is in the (very small) nucleus
the nucleus contains 5 protons and 6 neutrons; the electrons have negligible mass

pp.stem: The chemical properties of an element depend on the electronic configuration of its atoms.

parts.q: Give the full electronic configuration of a chlorine atom.
ms: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>5</sup>

parts.q: Deduce the number of pairs of electrons in the third shell (n = 3) of a sulfur atom.
ms: 2 (3s<sup>2</sup> is one pair; 3p<sup>4</sup> has one pair and two unpaired)

parts.q: State the shape of the highest-energy orbital that contains electrons in a potassium atom.
ms: spherical (4s)

parts.q: Write an equation to represent the first ionisation energy of oxygen.
ms: O(g) → O<sup>+</sup>(g) + e<sup>−</sup>

parts.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of oxygen is less than that of nitrogen.
ms: in O the electron is removed from a 2p orbital containing two electrons / a paired electron
spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove (N has three unpaired 2p electrons)

parts.q: Arrange Cl<sup>−</sup>, Ar and K<sup>+</sup> in order of increasing radius and explain your answer.
ms: K<sup>+</sup> < Ar < Cl<sup>−</sup>
all have the same number of electrons (18) / are isoelectronic
same shielding / same number of shells

pp.stem: This question is about the ions of some metals.

parts.q: Give the nucleon number, proton number and number of electrons in <sup>23</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> and <sup>24</sup>Mg<sup>2+</sup>.
State and explain the difference in ionic radius between Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup>.
